reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: A chalazion is a chronic, sterile lipogranulomatous swelling of a blocked meibomian gland, presenting as a firm, painless nodule within the tarsal plate
Unlike a stye (hordeolum), it is typically non-tender once the acute phase has passed and points towards the conjunctival rather than skin surface
It is strongly associated with blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction, and rosacea, and recurrences are common in these patients
A large chalazion can press on the cornea and induce astigmatism with blurred vision
Many small lesions resolve spontaneously or with conservative treatment using warm compresses and lid massage over several weeks
Persistent lesions are treated with incision and curettage through a conjunctival approach, or with intralesional steroid injection
A recurrent chalazion at the same site, or one with atypical features, should be biopsied to exclude sebaceous gland carcinoma
It should be distinguished from an internal hordeolum, which is an acute infective abscess of a meibomian gland
reference.pathophysiology: A chalazion forms when a meibomian gland orifice becomes obstructed and retained sebaceous secretions leak into the surrounding tarsal tissue. This lipid material provokes a chronic granulomatous (lipogranulomatous) inflammatory reaction rather than an infection, producing a firm nodule within the tarsal plate. Predisposing factors include meibomian gland dysfunction, blepharitis, and rosacea, all of which alter meibomian secretions and promote gland blockage.
additionalDifferentials: Sebaceous gland carcinoma of the eyelid
Basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma of the lid
additionalInvestigations: Clinical slit-lamp examination and eversion of the eyelid to assess the tarsal conjunctival surface
Refraction and assessment for induced astigmatism in large lesions
Histopathological examination of excised or curetted tissue in recurrent or atypical cases to exclude malignancy
redFlags: Recurrence at the same site or failure to resolve, raising suspicion of sebaceous gland carcinoma
Associated madarosis (lash loss), lid margin distortion, or induration suggesting malignancy
Rapid growth or ulceration of the overlying skin
Signs of secondary infection with spreading cellulitis
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; most chalazia resolve with conservative measures or minor surgery, though recurrences are common in patients with underlying meibomian gland disease. Rarely, a persistent or atypical lesion proves to be a malignancy, which is why histology is important in suspicious cases.
pitfalls: Assuming any recurrent lid nodule is benign and not sending atypical or recurrent lesions for histology
Confusing a sterile chalazion with an infective hordeolum and prescribing unnecessary antibiotics
Overlooking underlying blepharitis and meibomian gland dysfunction that drive recurrence
Missing chalazion-induced astigmatism as a cause of blurred vision
management: Treat initially with conservative measures using regular warm compresses and eyelid massage to express the retained meibomian secretions
Optimise eyelid hygiene and treat underlying blepharitis, meibomian gland dysfunction and rosacea to reduce recurrence
Offer intralesional corticosteroid injection for persistent lesions, particularly those near the lacrimal punctum
Perform incision and curettage through a conjunctival approach for lesions that fail to resolve
Assess for corneal astigmatism and visual disturbance in large lesions pressing on the globe
Send excised tissue for histopathology in recurrent or atypical lesions to exclude sebaceous gland carcinoma
